data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: The Bahamas effectively outsources monetary policy: the Bahamian dollar is pegged 1:1 to the US dollar, so inflation is largely imported and the central bank has little room for independent maneuver. Through the 2010s inflation stayed low, mostly 0-2.5%, with deflation of -0.3% in 2016 when oil prices collapsed and tourism softened. The only meaningful spike in the series was 2022, when post-COVID supply shocks and high fuel import costs pushed inflation to 5.6%, the period high; it then fell sharply to 0.4% in 2024 and a projected 0.6% in 2025, among the lowest readings in the dataset. The cost of the peg is vulnerability to imported price swings, which the introduction of VAT in 2015 also nudged up temporarily.
debt_management: Public debt was very low before the GFC, at 23.2% of GDP in 2006, but climbed relentlessly as repeated external shocks battered tourism revenues: 30.1% in 2009, 44.2% in 2013, 61.5% in 2018, with Hurricane Dorian (2019) and then COVID (GDP crashed from $13.28bn in 2019 to $10.36bn in 2020) pushing it to 90.7% of GDP in 2021, the series peak. The VAT introduced in January 2015 (7.5%, raised to 12% in 2018) strengthened revenues, and the post-COVID tourism rebound plus fiscal consolidation brought debt down to a projected 73.8% in 2025, well below the 2021 peak but triple the pre-GFC level. Debt remains largely external and denominated in USD, so rollover and climate shocks are the persistent risks rather than solvency.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis slashed US tourist spending; GDP dipped and debt rose from 25.3% to 30.1% of GDP.
Value Added Tax introduced at 7.5% in January 2015, anchoring the post-GFC fiscal consolidation effort.
Hurricane Matthew struck, damaging infrastructure and tourism receipts.
Hurricane Dorian devastated Grand Bahama and the Abacos, among the costliest Atlantic hurricanes on record.
COVID-19: border closures shut down tourism, the economy's engine; GDP fell to $10.36bn and debt jumped to 71.9% of GDP.
Post-COVID rebound plus global commodity shock pushed inflation to its 5.6% period peak.
Strong tourism recovery lifted GDP to a projected $16.51bn in 2025; debt eased back to 73.8% of GDP.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued tourism-led growth with very low inflation anchored by the USD peg, and a gradual debt decline if consolidation holds. The two structural risks are climate-driven hurricanes, which have twice in a decade reset the fiscal path, and dependence on US tourism and US monetary policy. Debt at ~74% of GDP is manageable for a small island economy, but another major hurricane or global travel shutdown would quickly reverse the gains.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
